Not comprehensively. All theories can be applied to all fields that are within the same scope but they cannot capture all the nuance of each field. Take for example rational choice theory. Rational choice theory is the theory (go figure) that people are rational actors (agency oddly enough is not required) who maximize their personal utility through limited options. This theory is great for economics. It can be applied to sociology, psychology, management, etc but it doesn't capture all the nuance of those fields. Much of the interplay between fields is delineating the inherent limitations of the basic principles of each field in regards to the primary questions of those fields. To the extent that a theory is fundamentally valid it should have strong descriptive/predictive abilities across fields but not perfect descriptive/predictive power across fields or even within a field. There are questions that economics has a hard time with (we aren't great with why people choose what they do internally just better at predicting what people will choice within set frameworks).
